extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, IP litigators, judges, and practitioners working with Korean patent/trademark law
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria used by the Korean Patent Court to evaluate patent validity, claim scope, doctrine of equivalents, description requirements (including Markush claims), prosecution history estoppel, negative scope confirmation actions, and related trademark/design registration issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description requirements for Markush-type claims (Article 42(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case where a claim of a medicinal invention is described as a Markush-type claim, even if some components of the selective elements thereof are not described as specific embodiments in the specification, if a person of ordinary skill in the art would not have had any difficulty in understanding and practicing the effect of the invention from the description of the specification and such effect can also be fully expected, such claim cannot be deemed to violate the description requirements of Article 42(3) of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on whether a person skilled in the art can understand and practice the invention's effect from the specification despite lack of explicit embodiments. The test is practical understandability and expectation of effect, not strict enumeration of every Markush member as specific embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest requirement for negative scope confirmation actions
rubrics_metrics.description: A negative scope confirmation action filed by a defendant immediately after an unfavorable-suspected infringement hearing may be deemed to have no interests in confirmation and thus be inadmissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors indicating lack of interest include: (1) the action merely seeks an interim confirmatory judgment duplicative of infringement proceedings (litigation economy); (2) there is no remaining insecurity or risk to be removed; (3) it imposes undue burden and costs on the patentee exercising rights; (4) it would enable circumvention of infringement proceedings; (5) it raises separation-of-powers concerns by using administrative trial during pending judicial infringement action; and (6) risk of contradictory judgments harming confidence in the patent system. Consider the whole factual context in assessing 'interest in confirmation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Public domain technology defense limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of public domain technology applies when the invention subject to confirmation merely consists of known technology or could have easily been practiced from known technology by a person of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, if the invention subject to confirmation includes all constitutional elements of a claim of the patented invention and thus literally infringes, the public domain technology principle is not applied. Use this as a restriction against expanding patent scope via doctrine of equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim scope is not necessarily limited by drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim's scope should not be limited to what is shown in the drawings merely because a particular embodiment in the drawings (e.g., 'formed of one frame') appears that way; drawings may illustrate embodiments but do not automatically limit claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claims by overall consideration of claim language, specification text (e.g., 'Constitution and Function of Invention'), and drawings. Determine whether drawing descriptions define a limitation or merely illustrate one way of implementing a feature. Example: 'bridge top face installing unit' interpreted by function (surface-contacting to support load) rather than being limited to a single-frame, curved structure shown in drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents / All Elements Rule applied flexibly
rubrics_metrics.description: In assessing equivalence between claim elements and accused or compared features, the 'All Elements Rule' may be applied flexibly in light of the essential technical idea and the theory of solving the problem in the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider factors including: (a) whether the inventions share the same theory of solving the problem (same essential technical idea); (b) possibility and easiness of substitution/modification by a person of ordinary skill in the art; (c) whether the difference affects function or effect (substantial functional equivalence); and (d) whether a difference is merely an additional limitation in a dependent claim rather than part of the essential technical idea. Use overall consideration of specification and publicly known technology at filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same theory of solving the problem (equivalence factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the subject patent and the compared invention embody the same essential technical idea or theory of solving the problem addressed by the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review the specification's statement of objectives and unique solving means; if both inventions implement the same core solution (e.g., separating parts to facilitate manufacture and replacement), differences in non-essential features may still be equivalent. Distinguish essential technical ideas from additional dependent-claim matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility and easiness of substitution (equivalence factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: If forming a feature by alternative means (e.g., curving vs welding; triangular plate vs inclined continuous member) would have been obvious or easily conceived by a person of ordinary skill, the features may be considered equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the alternative would have been selected as a matter of routine skill, whether it changes function/effect, and whether it was known in the art. If substitution is obvious and does not change function, equivalence is more likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional effect comparison (equivalence factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether differing structural features produce the same substantial functional effects claimed by the patent (e.g., reinforcement in multiple directions vs only one direction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the accused device lacks the claimed functional advantages (e.g., only strengthens panel in one direction rather than both), it may not be within the equivalent scope. The presence or absence of the improved functional effect can be decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history estoppel (doctrine applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee obtained the patent by limiting claim language during prosecution (e.g., limiting a feature's height), prosecution history estoppel can preclude the patentee from later claiming scope intentionally excluded during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine prosecution file history to see what claim scope was surrendered. If the patentee narrowed a claim to obtain allowance, under estoppel the patentee may be barred from recapturing the surrendered scope (e.g., feature heights lower than amended claim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential technical idea as determinant of inventive scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential technical idea of a patent (the unique solving means that cannot be found in prior art) is central to determining whether a compared invention shares the same inventive concept and thus whether elements are equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the characteristic features that embody the patent's unique technical idea (e.g., particular combination and orientation of embossed patterns that improve panel strength in multiple directions). If the compared device lacks that essential combination/effect, it will not be considered equivalent even if some individual features are known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark distinctiveness / descriptiveness test (Article 6(1)3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mark that consists only of marks indicating quality and effect of the designated goods in a normal way of use does not have distinctiveness and is a descriptive mark, not eligible for registration under Article 6(1)3 of the Trademark Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the mark in context (consumer recognition, prior market use). Example: '360do BRUSH' for toothbrushes was held descriptive because consumers understood it as meaning 'toothbrush with 360-degree bristles' given prior use and ordinary meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuous geographical name criterion for trademarks
rubrics_metrics.description: A geographical name used by many people in a specified region can be considered a 'conspicuous geographical name' even if it is not notably known nationwide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider evidence such as river/administrative names, many businesses using the name in the region, local stations/markets named accordingly, and local recognition of the name as denoting a product (e.g., 'Sincheon' in Daegu associated with spicy tteokbokki). Regional prominence can be sufficient to bar trademark protection as a geographical name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity to national or allied nation's flag (trademark rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: A trademark similar to the flag of an allied nation may be rejected under Article 7(1)1-2 if the mark shares common features—color arrangement and proportions—and the added element is small so the overall impression remains similar to the flag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare color order, geometric arrangement, aspect ratio, and relative size of any added device (e.g., a small hot-air balloon). Even small additions may not avoid similarity if the overall visual impression remains dominated by flag-like elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence test for trademarks containing names/titles of persons (Article 7(1)6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mark containing the name, title, portrait, or other identifying sign of a prominent person is not registrable; prominence is judged by period, manner, type and frequency of use, scope of trading, reality of trading, and whether the name has become widely recognized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess factual indicators of fame and public recognition in the relevant market and time; absence of such indicators means the prohibition may not apply (example: 'TIARA' not held to include name of girl group 'T-ara').
